posts.content:
Most people don't know why after every period of success is followed by a series of self-sabotaging actions that bring them back exactly where they started. And the reason is SELF-IMAGE.

No matter how hard you worked, you will never outperform your identity. The subconscious mind is so creative it will find ways to return you to what's familiar, which is your old life.

How to break the loop?

Start with the mind.

Install the identity and beliefs that are aligned with the life that you want to create.

The right action is an effect of the right mindset.

Then the pulling force that brought you down will start to push you up to live the life that you want to live.

posts.title:
Intvw with Lee Ainslie of Maverick, Graham & Doddsville, 2014 -- five excerpts on L/S equity, talent, and "No Holds" portfolio construction

1. Tiger Mindset - 'you should be the smartest person alive
posts.content:
Intvw with Lee Ainslie of Maverick, Graham & Doddsville, 2014 -- five excerpts on L/S equity, talent, and "No Holds" portfolio construction

1. Tiger Mindset - 'you should be the smartest person alive on your sector.'

"At Tiger you were essentially expected to be the foremost authority on a small number of stocks. For the investments you oversaw, no other public investor should know more about those companies than you did."

2. Talent evaluation: 

"The most important components we gauge include competitiveness, mental flexibility and emotional consistency—that last trait is surprisingly important. 

This is a very stressful business. We are all human, and we all make mistakes. How one responds to those mistakes and whether someone can keep a level head and make thoughtful decisions is critical. 

Conversely, how does one respond to a few big wins? With some folks, early success leads to inflated confidence that may slow the recognition of a mistake."

3. On 'No-Holds' Portfolio Management in L/S: 

"I think I have read almost everything that Warren Buffett has written, and I agree with more than 95% of his thinking, but this is one area where I disagree. 

I understand the tax impact of turnover, but nevertheless, I would argue that an investor should be able to overcome the negative tax consequences of shorter-term holdings through more efficient use of capital. 

For example, if I am starting a new fund, and my portfolio is a blank sheet of paper then I will evaluate the potential return of every potential investment from the prices the market is offering that day. I can decide how much risk I am willing to take to achieve expected returns, and I can evaluate how each opportunity compares to every other opportunity to develop a portfolio which I believe represents the optimal use of capital. 

In my view, tomorrow, I should go through the exact same process taking into account any new information including changes in the price of securities. If I conclude that a different portfolio would be preferable then I should buy or sell securities to get to the portfolio that I believe represents the optimal use of capital once again."

4. No-Holds (continued): 

"The “no holds” concept simply reflects the approach that every investment should represent a very compelling risk/reward opportunity from current prices, and if that’s not the case then that capital should be redeployed into positions that are viewed as very compelling at current prices. 

In the perfect world, every member of our investment team is pounding the table to increase the size their positions every day until they are at a maximum size in terms liquidity or risk contribution. 

When somebody tells me that they don’t think we should sell a stock, but that they wouldn't buy more at the current price either, then that investment probably does not represent one of our very best uses of capital—unless the size of the position is already at a maximum from a risk perspective. 

We want our portfolio invested in the most attractive use of capital today at current price points, and if a certain position no longer represents that then we should sell. 

Sometimes, people have a hard time with this because this philosophy often means we are reducing or exiting a position before it’s reached our expected price. For example, if a stock is 10% away from our original target price, we are likely to sell because we think there are many other opportunities with greater upside. 

Conceptually, our team has to accept this concept of “no holds.”

5. On Valuation

"To be clear, I think that valuation is a critical component of understanding where investment opportunities may lie. But I think many “value investors” purely focus on that metric and may ignore other important considerations. 

It’s one thing if you have a very cheap stock and reasons to believe that the cheap valuation will not persist: there's a new management team, there's an activist shareholder, they’re restructuring, they just made a decision to buy back stock, and so forth. I believe it is important to identify a catalyst that should benefit the valuation. 

The approach of simply identifying a very cheap stock that often has been cheap for a while and then just crossing your fingers and hoping the world will wake up and be willing to assign a higher valuation one day soon is not a very effective approach in my judgment. 

So while we place great emphasis on valuation in our investment decisions, valuation alone should never be the driver of either a long or a short investment."

END: Advice to students interested in an investing career

"Two things: first, read a lot. Read as many investment books as you can get your hands on. I've been able to learn something from almost every book I have ever read.

Secondly, the path to an investment career is not necessarily to work at a hedge fund or at a large mutual fund complex. You can start your career by simply improving your understanding of how different industries or companies work or how Wall Street works. Any brokerage firm or Wall Street firm can be a path to an investment career. A lot of people move from the sell-side to the buy-side over time. We probably have as many former McKinsey consultants as we do former Morgan Stanley investment bankers."

[link: https://t.co/dQXK8ha4ki]

The most brutal thing to understand about life is that you don't get what you want, you get what you believe you deserve.

You can do everything right. You can get the opportunity, the money, the rela
posts.content:
The most brutal thing to understand about life is that you don't get what you want, you get what you believe you deserve.

You can do everything right. You can get the opportunity, the money, the relationship, the dream handed to you on a plate. But if underneath it all you still don't believe you deserve good things, your mind treats the good life as a mistake that needs correcting. To your brain, a gap between reality and what you feel you deserve isn't success, it's an error, and your subconscious works to close that gap by pulling reality back down to match.

This is why people self-sabotage right when things start going well. The good relationship shows up and they pick fights or push the person away. The money comes in and somehow leaks back out within a year. It doesn't look like sabotage in the moment, it feels like bad luck or things just not working out. But it's too consistent to be bad luck. It's the feeling of not deserving it, dragging them back to what they think they're worth.

And this happens even when life completely changes on its own. Lottery winners go broke. People lose the weight and gain it back. People escape a toxic relationship and end up with someone just like the one they left. Everything around them changed, but the feeling of what they were worth stayed the same, so they ended up right back where it started.

that advice died in 1971 and nobody bothered to tell you. in 1971, nixon took the dollar off the gold standard and from that day, money stopped being tied to gold. the entire game shifted overnight but your parents, your teachers and your financial advisors kept teaching the old rules.

the people who followed that advice spent their lives wondering why they couldn't get ahead, meanwhile they were all playing the wrong game.

my dad followed every rule he was given, worked hard, saved carefully, did everything right and still hit the same ceiling every single year cos the rules he followed were designed for a different era. meanwhile, his filthy rich brother thought differently. every time the rules changed, he noticed. he studied the new game and moved before everyone else figured it out.

that's how wealth is built, not by working harder inside a broken system but by recognizing when the game shifts and moving first.

the rules just changed again.

ai has done to business what 1971 did to money. everything is different now and most people don't know it yet.

for the first time in history, one person can build and run an entire business without employees, without massive capital, and without showing up every single day. content, sales and customer service can all run without you. the people who recognize this now are the ones who win. the people who wait will spend the next decade wondering what happened.

follow the trend, follow the money.
learn, buena suerte 👍

just last month, i asked one of my associate who built a fortune what really separated him from everyone else.

tho i've been watching how he lived. i noticed what others called balance, he called it distraction and while others waited for motivation, he relied on discipline. when everyone else quit after the 10th failure, he treated it like the 10th lesson and when people laughed at his vision, he kept acting as tho the future he imagined already existed and right there before him staring at him.

at that point i clocked it that every wealthy person i know shares exactly these same 4 traits, i do too: they're obsessed enough to outwork the average, disciplined enough to stay consistent, relentless enough to survive rejection and just delusional enough to believe they can create a life everyone else thinks is impossible.

okay now, use elon as an reference and case study here, elon still shows up every single day, regardless of being the richest man on earth, statistically. man is still obsessed with growth, building and progress, moving like this is just the tip of his iceberg.

that's the mindset, learn something 👍

1. Visualize. As Ali’s friend notes, when you’re tackling a big goal, visualize it. What does success look like? Failure? What happens the d
posts.content:
Extremely powerful lesson: You can simply stop complaining

1. Visualize. As Ali’s friend notes, when you’re tackling a big goal, visualize it. What does success look like? Failure? What happens the day after you accomplish it?

2. Create rules. I have a personal rule: I’m not allowed to complain about the price of anything. I can afford it and I’m an adult who makes spending choices with my eyes wide open. 

3. (Most important) Build the skill of refocusing on a new feeling, not simply reducing complaining. This takes deep psychological work. What are you getting out of complaining? (Think really deeply: What are you getting out of sighing loudly when you get up from a deep chair? Or venting to a friend, or even rolling your eyes when you see the bill at your neighborhood restaurant?) I suggest GRATITUDE: “I’m thankful I can afford to pay this and help provide for other people’s livelihood”

This is a core part of living a Rich Life

posts.content:
proof that you can be smart but terrible at creating wealth.

one of my relatives was in the armed forces.

at his prime, he was making more than 1L+.

whenever he used to visit my home, he used to come with full rich vibes.

new phone, new car, new jewellery, etc.

he changed many houses.

everything was going well but one day he RETIRED.

his salary STOPPED.

now at this point, he had only 1 income source and a family of 6 people (parents + 4 kids).

also by the time he retired, only one of his kid completed his education (out of 4).

to make things worse, he didn't focus much on the future of his kids (i mean he did but only money wise. didn't focus on their mindset).

so his eldest son doesn't make any money. and worst case, he got married so now there are a total 5 kids to take care of.

also his son was blessed with a daughter last year so totaling 8 people — parents + 6 kids

they live in a tier 2 city. 3 of the kids are still in school. and 3 of them (his eldest son + his wife + their daughter) is a family in itself with 0 income, and the overall income source is only one. 35k. a month.

so now he does one more job to sustain the expenses.

but here's a weird dilemma: his expenses are so high that he can't build an extra income source.

and because he can't build any extra income source, his expenses will always remain high.

it's a fatal trap. and most indians fall into it.

in my opinion, these are the mistakes he made:

- he never learnt about a particular field to work in after retirement. he always had the mindset of pouring money into something and it'll just work.

- gave up too soon. he tried many things like farming, trading of grains, etc but gave up on the slightest problem. never persisted enough.

- poor financial knowledge. he never understood how money works. never understood assets and liabilities and the basics of managing money.

- vision. he never tried to foresee the future and upcoming possible problems. this led to poor decisions.

posts.title: Norway wins the most medals at the Winter Olympics, with a population of just 5.6 million. People say it’s because Norway is a winter wonderland, but they’re also elite at triathlon, beach volleyball,
posts.content:
Norway wins the most medals at the Winter Olympics, with a population of just 5.6 million. People say it’s because Norway is a winter wonderland, but they’re also elite at triathlon, beach volleyball, cycling, and as the world is now seeing, soccer.

A big part of their success is how they treat youth sports—and it’s the opposite of what we do in the US and Canada. Here’s what we can learn from Norway:

1. Scorekeeping:

In the US: Youth sports tend to be hyper competitive even at early ages. Leagues almost always keep score.

In Norway: Scorekeeping isn’t even allowed until age 13.

Removing winners and losers keeps the focus on the process not outcomes. It keeps kids engaged longer because it minimizes pressure (and tears) and maximizes fun, learning, and growth. The goal isn’t to win a third grade championship. It’s to love sport and keep playing.

2. Trophies:

In the US: If you give everyone a trophy, you’re creating snowflakes who will never gain a competitive edge.

In Norway: Whenever trophies are awarded, they are handed out to everyone.

If getting a trophy makes young kids feel good, we should give them trophies. Maybe they’ll come back and play again next year!!

As for the creation of snowflakes with no competitive edge—Norway’s athletes are tough as nails and all they do is win.

3. Prioritizing Fun:

In the US: Far too often, the goal is to win.

In Norway: The national philosophy is “joy of sport.”

Youth sports in the US are driven by adults, ego, and money. Youth sports in Norway are driven by fun.

Only half of kids in the US participate in sports. The number one reason they drop out: because they aren’t having fun anymore. In Norway, 93% of kids participate in youth sports. Fun is the foremost goal.

4. Playing Multiple Sports:

In the US: There’s pressure to specialize early and play your best sport year round.

In Norway: Try as many sports as you can before specializing as late as college.

Norway encourages kids to try all types of sport. This reduces injury and burnout and increases all-around athleticism. It also helps promotes match quality, or finding the sport you are best suited for as your body develops, which is impossible if you commit to a single sport too early.

5. Affordability

In the US: There is increasingly a pay-to-play model with high fees for leagues, equipment, and travel. This excludes many kids from playing.

In Norway: It’s a national priority to keep youth sports affordable and therefore accessible for all.

Kids aren’t priced out, which creates opportunities for everyone to participate (and develop into athletes), regardless of their parents’ income level.

Norway’s sporting success isn’t just speculation or a nice story. A large body of research supports their approach:

• Studies show athletes who specialize later in life have a significantly higher chance of becoming elite.
• Soccer players whose motivation is primarily internal (versus external) have more than a 3x better chance of making it to an elite level.
• The number one predictor of whether or not kids stay in sport is are they having fun.
• Parents connect winning to having fun whereas kids say having fun is about being with their friends and learning.

We could learn a lot from Norway:

In the US, 70% of kids drop out of youth sports by age 13. This not only diminishes an elite-athlete pipeline, but it also destroys an opportunity for healthy habits and all the character lessons kids can learn from sport.

In Norway, lifelong participation in sport is the norm. The goal isn’t to have the best 9U team. It’s to develop the best athletes. Those are two very different things. And Norway has the medals to prove it.

I don’t know if I’ve made this clear enough, but…

Oscar and Zeta are my two biggest holdings across all of my investment portfolios.

When I find real conviction in a company, I back it with serious
posts.content:
I don’t know if I’ve made this clear enough, but…

Oscar and Zeta are my two biggest holdings across all of my investment portfolios.

When I find real conviction in a company, I back it with serious capital.

I did it with Tesla.
I did it with Meta.
I did it with AXP.
I did it with Google.

And now I’m doing it again.

Some people talk about a lot of stocks and only take tiny positions.

That ain’t me.

I trade multiple positions separately, but when it comes to investing, I hammer down on my highest conviction ideas.

Of course I own other stocks. Of course I like other companies.

But the biggest chunks of capital go to the names I believe have the biggest long-term opportunity.

That’s why I share my thoughts, ideas, research, and analysis with you all.

I’ve been doing this since I started posting consistently back in late 2024 because I genuinely love trading and investing.

I’m passionate about teaching what I’ve had to learn the hard way over the last 10+ years.

And more than anything, I want to help my friends put themselves in a position to build a better life for their families.

I’m just a guy who came from nothing and wanted more.

I joined the Air Force to get out of a bad environment.

I self-taught myself finance, trading, and investing.

And by the grace of God, I was eventually able to provide for my family through my passion, leave the military, and become my own boss.

Anyone can do it.

You just have to work for it, stay consistent, and keep showing up.

All praise to God for any success I’ve had.

And I hope I’m able to help you all somewhere along your journey.

…yes I use to shave my head and yes my wife is beautiful.

Much love,
Ronnie

posts.content:
JOKES

I strongly disagree.

Living with my parents has probably been one of the biggest advantages I've had.

I don't pay rent. Because of that, I've had the freedom to make mistakes, try different things, take risks, learn new skills, build projects, and create opportunities for other people.

I've worked with world-class projects, including Webtoons and fintech companies in the US, all from my parents' house.

I've been invited to speak at events in places I've never been before. I've partnered with amazing founders and professionals. I've helped people get their first opportunities. And I did all of that without the pressure of wondering how I'll pay ₦2 million in rent next year.

Some people make a little money and immediately start preaching that everyone should move out. That's terrible advice for many young people.

What happens when the income becomes unstable?

What happens when you don't know where the next client is coming from?

What happens when rent, feeding, transportation, and bills start competing with your dreams?

Many people would never have built anything meaningful if they had those pressures too early.

The truth is, not paying rent gives you something incredibly valuable: time and runway.

Time to learn.
Time to network.
Time to experiment.
Time to fail.
Time to build.

You can literally sit in your parents' house, work with people across the world, attend meetings from your phone, build a business, create jobs, and impact lives. LITERALLY WHAT I AM DOING. 

Some of you will move out and still be introverted. You'll still stay indoors. You'll still have the same habits. Changing location doesn't automatically change your life.

If you're going to change your life, it has to come from you. You have to be audacious. You have to create opportunities. You have to take action.

A rented apartment doesn't create ambition. Ambition creates ambition.

Move out when it makes sense for your finances, your growth, and your goals, not because somebody on the internet convinced you that suffering is a prerequisite for success.

posts.title:
If you told me 10-15 years ago that I’d pay off all my student debt, retire my wife, and build the life I’m living now, I wouldn’t have believed you.

Not because I didn’t want those things badly enou
posts.content:
If you told me 10-15 years ago that I’d pay off all my student debt, retire my wife, and build the life I’m living now, I wouldn’t have believed you.

Not because I didn’t want those things badly enough, but because the version of me back then wasn’t capable of doing it.

That guy was still treating trading like a casino, taking impulsive trades, and had no real structure.

He didn’t have the discipline.

He didn’t have the experience.

He didn’t have the mindset.

And to be completely honest, he just didn’t have the knowledge or skills to achieve that type of success.

From that point of view, to think that I could become a full-time trader made no sense.

And that’s the mistake most traders make.

They limit what they can do in the future based on where they are now.

They sit where they are today and ask:

How am I going to do all of this? 

How am I going to make it work? 

How am I going to get to that level when I keep messing up?

They base their future potential on their current flaws.

But the version of you that’s crushing it in the markets is not the same version of you reading this right now, full of doubt, frustration, impatience, and habits that still need to be broken. 

That version of you is a completely different person.

And as hard as it is to believe right now, from them, making money in the markets is pretty easy.

That future version of you won’t appear overnight. 

They’re created little by little through the process.

So stop obsessing over how you’re going to pull off the end result from where you are right now.

That is not your job.

Your only job is to become the person who can.

Because once you become that person, the results that feel impossible to you today start feeling like the easiest thing in the world.

posts.title:
i just got off a call with the man behind all of @moonpay's social media accounts.

he's pulling in north of 100m views every month across X, Instagram, Linkedin, and Tiktok.

i genuinely consider him
posts.content:
i just got off a call with the man behind all of @moonpay's social media accounts.

he's pulling in north of 100m views every month across X, Instagram, Linkedin, and Tiktok.

i genuinely consider him to be one of the legends in this space, and i wanted to share 6 of the biggest lessons he gave me about growing an audience on X.

unlike the other big brand in the crypto scene (won't name but yk who I'm talking abt)

moonpay has managed to become one of the most recognizable and more importantly one of the most liked brands in crypto.

let's get into it:

1. post more, think less

this is obviously a given and one of my favorite sayings. context on x has a short life span, people see your post and forget about it the next day, the key is to post a lot and the good posts naturally  rise to the top.

2. more storytelling, less product

i'm in charge of growing the flex X account, so this was actually super valuable to me.

i've mostly been posting only product content, but he suggested talking more about the story behind flex and leaning into invoking emotions and feelings rather than just features.

for us, that means speaking more about our tagline, "flex fuels ambition" and sharing more of that path to success that flex enables.

3. there is no perfect time to post

i already knew this, but hearing it from the man behind moonpay reinforced it.

the myth that there's a magical posting time is bullshit.

i've had posts go viral at 2am and i've had posts go viral in the middle of the afternoon.

for X at least, timing matters far less than most people think.

4. engage with every single person

sounds obvious but this tip has a lot of psychology rooted into it.

people are on social media because they want to be validated and seen. they want attention.

when a big brand account with a gold checkmark likes a post or replies to a comment, it builds a surprising amount of what I like to call "relationship equity".

over time these interactions compound into immense brand affinity.

my own little tip of advice to throw in here is to always respond with a question to prolong the talk.

when someone responds and the conversation continues x sees genuine back and forth engagement rather than a one off interaction.

the X algo eats this shit up like crazy and increases reach.

5. you don't need a big team

i assumed moonpay had a social team of 5-10 people.

wrong.

it's essentially Sean himself and one other girl helping manage everything.

they produce dozens of pieces of content everyday on top of interacting with thousands of people across 4 different social channels.

I struggle keeping up with just mine and the flex account  and was thinking of getting an assistant, hearing that Sean does this all basically by himself was insane to me.

6. be chronically online

his final piece of advice was simple, be chronically online. active at all times during the day.

could be posting, replying, commenting, dming, literally anything.

growing a  brand really comes down to just an insane volume output of good quality content.

key word good. not excellent. 

the more people you engage with, the more people know you which means the more people like you.

getting 30 minutes of his time to learn how he thinks about growing brands at scale was incredibly valuable.

I also want to point out I offered to pay Sean a consultation fee for his time and he declined, instead opting in to helping me out for free.

absolute legend. @PackripEwing
